title: Atrial Fibrillation: From Discovery of AF Mechanisms to DOACs and Catheter Ablation

content.intro: Atrial fibrillation (AF) has a rich history dating back to the 18th century. The first description of AF is attributed to Jean-Baptiste de Sénac in 1749. However, it was not until the early 20th century that the condition gained significant attention. In 1906, Sir James Mackenzie described a case of 'auricular fibrillation' in the British Medical Journal. The introduction of electrocardiography (ECG) in the 1900s revolutionized the diagnosis of AF. In 1909, Willem Einthoven, a Dutch physiologist, published the first ECG recording of AF, earning him the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1924. The 1960s and 1970s saw significant advancements in the understanding of AF mechanisms, with landmark papers by researchers such as Maurice Sokolow and Albert L. Waldo. The development of catheter ablation in the 1990s marked a new era in AF treatment.

lessons.title: Pathophysiology and Aetiology of Atrial Fibrillation

content.intro: Atrial fibrillation is characterized by rapid and irregular atrial contractions, resulting in a loss of atrial contraction and an irregular ventricular response. The pathophysiology of AF involves complex molecular mechanisms, including alterations in ion channels, calcium handling, and fibrosis. Genetic factors, such as mutations in the KCNQ1 and SCN5A genes, can also contribute to the development of AF. There are several subtypes of AF, including paroxysmal, persistent, and permanent AF, each with distinct characteristics and treatment approaches. The aetiology of AF is multifactorial, involving factors such as age, hypertension, heart disease, and lifestyle.

content.intro: Atrial fibrillation can present with a range of symptoms, including palpitations, shortness of breath, fatigue, and chest pain. The cardinal symptoms of AF are palpitations and shortness of breath, which occur in approximately 70% of patients. The clinical presentation of AF can vary depending on the subtype, with paroxysmal AF often presenting with sudden onset of symptoms and persistent AF presenting with more gradual onset. Atypical presentations of AF can include asymptomatic AF, which is estimated to occur in up to 30% of patients. The stages of AF include new-onset, paroxysmal, persistent, and permanent AF, each with distinct treatment approaches.

content.intro: Atrial fibrillation (AF) diagnosis involves a combination of clinical evaluation, electrocardiography (ECG), and imaging studies. The diagnosis is typically made using a 12-lead ECG, which shows irregular fibrillatory waves and an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm. The CHA2DS2-VASc score is used to assess the risk of stroke in patients with AF. Laboratory tests, such as thyroid function tests and electrolyte panels, may be ordered to rule out underlying conditions that may be contributing to AF. Echocardiography is also commonly used to evaluate left ventricular function and to identify any underlying structural heart disease.

content.intro: The treatment of atrial fibrillation (AF) involves a combination of pharmacological and non-pharmacological strategies. Pharmacological treatment options include anti-arrhythmic medications, such as flecainide and propafenone, and anticoagulants, such as warfarin and direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs). Non-pharmacological treatment options include catheter ablation, which involves the use of radiofrequency energy to destroy the abnormal electrical pathways in the heart that are causing AF. Other non-pharmacological treatment options include pacemaker implantation and cardioversion.

content.intro: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is associated with an increased risk of complications, including stroke, heart failure, and mortality. The risk of stroke in AF patients can be estimated using the CHA2DS2-VASc score, and anticoagulation therapy is recommended for patients with a high risk of stroke. Heart failure is also a common complication of AF, and treatment should be aimed at controlling ventricular rate and improving cardiac function. The prognosis of AF patients is generally poor, with a significant increase in mortality and morbidity.

content.intro: Atrial fibrillation (AF) can occur in special populations, including pediatric and elderly patients, and pregnant women. In these populations, treatment should be individualized based on patient-specific factors. Emerging therapies for AF include new anti-arrhythmic medications and catheter ablation techniques. Pipeline drugs, such as vernakalant and ranolazine, are being developed for the treatment of AF. Additionally, advances in catheter ablation technology, such as robotic navigation and contact force sensing, are improving the efficacy and safety of the procedure.
